#6423. Scientists Discover That One Simple Desk Change Could Boost Productivity by Nearly $9,000 a Year

The desk you work at may have more influence on productivity than you think, with research involving over 10,000 employees linking standing desks to greater daily computer activity.

For anyone who spends most of the workday in front of a computer, sitting for hours can leave the back aching, the neck stiff, and energy running low by midafternoon. Standing up and moving around can help break up that routine, which is part of the appeal of height-adjustable desks. These workstations let employees switch between sitting and standing without stepping away from their work, offering a simple way to reduce physical strain and spend less time in one position.

Now, a large study from Texas A&M University suggests that sit-stand desks may offer another advantage. Employees using them averaged about 43 more minutes of active computer use each day than those working at traditional desks. Over a year, that difference could represent nearly $9,000 in potential productivity value per employee.

The research, published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics, was co-led by Dr. Mark Benden, a professor at Texas A&M’s School of Public Health, and Dr. Tricia Salzar, Regional Ergonomist for the U.S. Army Public Health Command Region, West.

Rather than relying on a small laboratory experiment, the researchers examined how people used their computers during ordinary workdays. “We analyzed a huge dataset of more than 10,000 workers over a yearlong period, comparing the total computer use of traditional desk users and height-adjustable desk users,” Benden said.

The team combined employee comfort surveys with software measurements of computer activity, including keystrokes, words typed, mouse clicks, and typing errors. This allowed the researchers to examine both how workers felt about their workstations and how actively they used their computers.

“It was important that we collected subjective measurements, like employee survey responses of their comfort and objective measurements of computer activity through software, to analyze how people engaged with their work,” Benden said.

Employees with sit-stand desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time per day, compared with 2.95 hours among those using conventional desks. That difference of approximately 43 minutes may seem modest during a single workday, but the researchers calculated that it amounted to roughly 171 additional hours annually, equivalent to more than four 40-hour workweeks.

The difference also extended beyond time spent using a computer. Employees with adjustable desks generally typed more words and recorded more keystrokes, suggesting that the additional activity was accompanied by greater measurable output.

“The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way,” Benden said.

Using a standardized hourly wage of approximately $52, the researchers calculated that those 171 additional hours could represent nearly $9,000 in annual productivity value for each employee. The figure is an estimate based on computer activity and hourly wages, rather than a demonstrated increase in company profits or a financial return that accounts for the cost of purchasing the desks.

“Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” Benden said.

The results are encouraging, although the comparison does not establish that the desks themselves caused the difference in activity. The measurements also do not directly show whether employees experienced less back pain, reduced fatigue, or better concentration. Those remain potential benefits rather than outcomes established by the reported computer-use findings.

Still, the results add to a broader discussion about how the spaces people work in can influence their daily experience. Employers often look to new software, training, and management strategies to improve performance, while the physical surroundings receive less attention.

“It’s what we call the ‘workplace effect,’” Benden said. “The direct impact that the physical work environment has on the behavior, health, psychological well-being, and even engagement and performance of employees.”

A sit-stand desk is a relatively straightforward example of that idea. Instead of requiring someone to remain seated throughout the day, it allows them to adjust their position as their comfort and tasks change. For workers who spend much of their time at a computer, that flexibility may make long workdays more manageable.

“It can have a profound effect,” Benden said. “Alternating between different working positions promotes better health outcomes by reducing physical strain and encouraging movement for those who might otherwise spend most of their workday sedentary.”

The possibility of easing physical discomfort while supporting more sustained energy and longer periods of focused work makes adjustable desks appealing to employees. For employers, the potential benefit is a workforce that can remain productive while working in a more comfortable environment.

“It has a cumulative, positive effect for both employers and employees,” Benden said.

Benden believes these findings demonstrate why workplace design deserves a larger role in conversations about employee health and organizational performance.

“The design of the workplace itself can be a powerful driver of human health and performance, including better engagement, productivity, and organizational success,” Benden said.

“The implications are hard to ignore,” Benden said. “When we design workplaces around employees and their needs, better health, better performance, and better organizational outcomes follow.”

Understanding that relationship has been a major focus of Benden’s career. A former Army Reserve officer, engineer, healthcare professional, inventor, and internationally recognized researcher, he has spent decades investigating how work environments affect the people who use them.

“We spend a lot of time at work,” Benden said. “It’s my passion to make sure that workers feel supported in their workplace, built on informed and guided scientific evidence.”

He currently directs the Center for Worker Health at Texas A&M, which brings together engineering, management, and technology through interdisciplinary research, innovation, and education. Its work focuses on developing practical improvements in worker health and efficiency, while helping students turn their ideas into real-world applications.

“The Center partners with industry nationwide, to develop innovative, impactful systems and practices that have a direct effect on worker health and efficiency,” Benden said. “We also train students and give them the platform to be as creative as possible to turn new ideas into impactful applications.”

The research is also expanding beyond furniture and ergonomics. As artificial intelligence becomes a more common part of office work, Benden is interested in how these technologies might interact with the physical environments in which employees perform their jobs.

“Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into daily work,” Benden said. “Just as we’ve studied how the physical environment affects human health and performance, we’re interested in understanding how emerging AI technologies could influence the physical workspace and outcomes of organizations.”

For organizations considering changes to their offices, the findings suggest that improving the everyday experience of working at a computer may be worth examining alongside investments in new technology. Whether the goal is to reduce physical strain, encourage movement, or support productivity, even something as familiar as a desk could have a role to play.

“The next breakthrough may not come from working harder, but from designing workspaces and systems that help people work smarter and more efficiently,” Benden said.

Reference: “Improved Computer Utilization Associated with Height Adjustable Workstations in a Large Office Population” by Tricia Lynn Salzar, Matthew Lee Smith, Adam Pickens, Gang Han and Mark Edward Benden, 19 September 2026, Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics. DOI: 10.3390/tae2030021

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6421. Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Michigan woman uses a brain implant to speak with her neurosurgeon. Efforts to restore speech highlight what’s at stake when we lose opportunities to talk.

Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.

We’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.

And as season two wraps up, listeners will be left with a reminder of the power of a voice: a piece of comedy from Jules Rodriguez, performed with his voice clone in front of a live crowd.

“Being backstage and then seeing him come out, like, roll out his wheelchair, and everybody goes nuts because they’re like, ‘What is going on here? This doesn’t make sense,’” says Jules’ wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez. “And every time I was like, ‘This is life. This is love. This is passion. What else is there?’ I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here.”

Laura Sanders: OK, I want to ask who your favorite comedians are and why. Who makes you all laugh?

Jules Rodriguez: Pete Holmes and Mike Birbiglia are some of my favorites.

[Audio] He was just like, I’m a bear, et cetera.

[Audio] The best part of sleep is falling asleep. That’s the only part you’re there for.Jules: Their styles are different, but I have always gravitated towards their authenticity.

Sanders: There’s another comedian who is extra meaningful for Jules: Conan O’Brien.

[Audio] Today is a bit of a different sort of episode. I’ll be talking to Jules and Maria.

Sanders: After MA had reached out, Conan invited the couple onto his podcast, where they connected about comedy. Conan still checks in on Jules every so often.

[Audio] It’s incredible to me that in our conversations, you’re very frank about the pain that you go through, and how intense it is. But you’re also always so positive and funny and, frankly, you give me a lot of [beep]. Which I find to be, well I hate it, by the way, first of all. Oh, get over it, Conan.

Jules: Conan is very special to me. Watching and listening to him helped me disconnect from the harsh reality of my life. And when I got to meet him and chat with him, it meant the world to me.

Maria Aleandra Fernandez: Having the most normal conversation with Conan O’Brien is something I will never get over.

[Audio] So he has a bunch of banked phrases. He’s going to play a few of our favorites. OK. I’m fine. I’m perfectly [beep] fine. [laughter] Come on man, are we doing this or not? Oh my God, oh my God. I’m destroying this marriage. MA: He really is so genuine and like, not only willing to talk to us, but really looks forward to talking. Like, I love talking to you guys. I’m not just doing it to be a nice person, which feels, you know, feels wonderful.

[Audio] You have my love, my respect and we’re thinking about you guys all the time.

Sanders: As you were talking earlier, it made me think about what it means to make somebody laugh and to entertain them, and like how actually very, very special that must be. Just kind of, at its heart, it’s, it is joy and humans connecting. And so, extra special.

MA: That’s the other thing I’ve learned mainly through Jules, about humor and comedy. And who were we watching yesterday? The NPR interview with Dave Chappelle. [Audio] Dave Chappelle says he is very clear about his role as a comedian.

MA: And Dave Chappelle said something that is so spot-on. He said that comedians are how people metabolize things.

[Audio] We’re like the nation’s kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts, but feelings around facts, or ideas. And jokes are just a shorthand for all of that.

MA: And I’m also a nerd and I’ve been reading some Greek tragedies and studying about how, you know, that’s also like the artists that help people metabolize feelings and emotions. And when he said that, I was like, that’s exactly it. And that’s what Jules has done.

It’s something that heals. And it’s not even like it’s self-deprecating. It’s not like, oh, let’s make fun. And the way he does it is so smart and genuine, but also not taking himself seriously. It just disarms everything. You’re just like, oh, OK. And that idea of metabolizing the really hard feelings that come around grief, mortality, losing a person, seeing how he’s trapped in his body, but he chooses not to be trapped in that really big way is so profound.

Sanders: Science is iterative. It builds. It may take a wrong turn or two, but overall, it’s moving toward a deeper understanding of our world and of ourselves.

By using their voices, by telling their stories, by telling their jokes, Jules and MA are helping me, and maybe you too, metabolize the pain – and the joy – of living. Welcome to The Deep End, Talk to Me.

[Voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.

Sanders: I’m Laura Sanders and today, we’re going to look ahead to what’s coming next for the human voice and efforts to restore it.

Sanders: In some ways, this podcast is a story of progress, of figuring out, little by little, more about the brain, and more about technology and more about people. Today, Jules can type with his eyes, and his son can hear his dad’s voice say I love you. In earlier episodes, you heard from Casey Harrell. Casey can think about saying a word to his daughter, and boom, they’re off playing a game together.

Casey Harrell: So this has kept me still in touch with people and the world, and it is not hyperbole to frame it this way.

Sanders: Casey has ALS and can no longer speak. He volunteered for a clinical trial, and now he has a device implanted in his brain that detects neural patterns as he tries to say a word. This system has changed his life.

Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary.

Leigh Hochberg: In terms of actually decoding attempted speech, I’m almost sure it’s still less than 10. It may be closer to five or six, so far, and that number undoubtedly is going to increase fairly quickly.

Sanders: So this is a small but growing number. Growing, because we now have a solid scientific understanding of the brain’s speech signals, and other signals too. And neurotech companies are very interested.

Hochberg: About 10 years ago or so, the academic research had de-risked this field sufficiently that it allowed for the entry of now likely a dozen or more companies that are actively pursuing their own version of an implantable brain-computer interface.

What I anticipate will happen, what I guess I hope will happen, is that the companies will continue to very carefully, thoughtfully and in a very focused manner, create their systems, and test them rigorously. And hopefully they’ll be demonstrated to be safe and effective. And at the same time, the academic groups have the opportunity to continue to demonstrate what’s possible, to push beyond that, and to show hopefully what those medical devices, once they’re actually available to market, might be able to do next.

Sanders: I talked with Vikash Gilja, a neural engineer who works at a company called Paradromics. He sees this momentum that Hochberg describes too.

Vikash Gilja: And, you know, we can see all the pieces coming together. These tools weren’t available even five years ago. And what we’re seeing is like, you know, month over month, there are new tools available. So we’re able to leverage those and move faster.

Matthew Willsey: So the cortical module has 421 tiny little sensors.

Sanders: That’s neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer Matthew Willsey, of the University of Michigan Health. He’s describing the device from Paradromics here.

Willsey: They’re about one and a half millimeters long. And you know, it’s smaller than your thumbnail, like kind of all the way around. It’s like a cylinder. And at the bottom of the cylinder are the electrodes, is what we call them. And we get them really close to the brain. And then when we deploy it, what it does is it pushes those electrodes down into the brain.

Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

[Audio] I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. Yeah, it’s good.

When Casey uses his brain-computer interface, it decodes speech signals from his brain, then puts words on a screen. Casey then selects a button, using his eye movements or his brain-computer interface, to say these words out loud with a digital voice. Here’s Casey.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Sanders: But scientists want to skip this middle part — the words written on a screen. They want instead to go straight to speech, and perhaps make conversations faster. Casey says this goal to go directly from brain signals to a speaking digital voice would be his top priority.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

P., Gibson, M. C., Goodhead, I., Gubili, C., Hermosilla-Albala, N., Hrbek, T., Janiak, M. C., Kuderna, L. F. K., ... Boubli, J. P. (2026). Genome-wide analyses reveal recent diversification and hidden diversity in Amazonian howler monkeys, including two new species. Communications Biology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-026-11187-8

#6418. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) officially announced its decision to revoke the United States' measles elimination status on Nov. 17, 2026. The week prior, the Wall Street Journal reported that the PAHO had reached that decision.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6414. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

From an award-winning expert on DNA, discover the myth-busting book that opens a dazzling window into the world of modern genetics.

Fascinating, compassionate, and entirely captivating, The Secrets of Our DNA is the essential book that explains how genetics has changed and transformed the world around us.

Turi King is renowned for presenting complex findings on DNA and genetic science in an accessible and compelling way and she has won awards for her public engagement in science. Turi is the director of the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath. She is an honorary fellow of the British Science Association, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London, a member of the Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences, and a member of the International Society of Forensic Geneticists. She is well known for her academic work leading the identification of Richard III; advising on the case of Mary Jane Kelly (the last victim of Jack the Ripper); leading the project on sequencing Hitler’s genome; as well as her media work co-presenting BBC’s DNA Family Secrets.

#6412. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

#6410. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.
