Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

Clarissa Brincat is a freelance writer specializing in health and medical research. After completing an MSc in chemistry, she realized she would rather write about science than do it. She learned how to edit scientific papers in a stint as a chemistry copyeditor, before moving on to a medical writer role at a healthcare company. Writing for doctors and experts has its rewards, but Clarissa wanted to communicate with a wider audience, which naturally led her to freelance health and science writing. #6408. Subway Workers Dug Under a Busy Street and Found an Ancient City of the Dead

Archaeologists say the Roman-era body count is still climbing.

Digging under Calle Hilera, a busy street in Málaga, Spain, is bound to churn up remnants of the seaside city’s past. Officials just didn’t expect those remnants to be the literal remains of more than 1,000 people from the Roman era.

During a project to extend the local metro line toward a future hospital site, crews exposed 984 burial complexes holding the remains of more than 1,000 people, according to the regional ministry of public works, as reported by Sur.

The finds began piling up in the spring. When the discovery was first announced, the metro authority had uncovered 600 burials. Since then, the count has climbed past 1,000 individuals, and officials expect it to keep rising. So far, investigations have revealed a wide variety of burial types, but all of them date from the second to fourth centuries C.E., when the Romans were dominant along the Iberian Peninsula’s coastline.

Although the crews found relatively few grave goods (mainly the expected pottery, coins, and a smattering of personal items), the necropolis, which stretches roughly 1,300 feet, has proven rich in other ways. Mario Muñoz-Atanet, the regional government’s public works delegate in Málaga, told Sur that the number of graves will likely grow as excavations continue.

The burials include tile-lined tombs, table-style tombs, and a range of simple pits. In a few cases, newborns were buried inside amphorae. Many graves were also reused. “We are working on them one by one, tomb by tomb,” Muñoz-Atanet said. “One tomb of each type will be displayed in the future metro archaeology museum.”

According to Muñoz-Atanet, plans for that museum are already underway, and finds from the metro excavations will form the centerpiece of its collection.

The burial site also lies close to where the Nasrid Wall was discovered. That wall was built by the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled the last Islamic kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula from the 13th to the 15th centuries, long after the Roman-era burials. Experts believe that in the second century, the necropolis sat well outside the city but along a key coastal route leading out of the urban center. The site may even have been underwater in the centuries before it became a burial ground.

The excavations have also turned up coins from many different places. According to Muñoz-Atanet, these coins help confirm Málaga’s history as a port that drew people from all over.

That cosmopolitan past is no surprise. Málaga has passed through the hands of many rulers, and the modern city is built atop Phoenician, Roman, and Moorish settlements. Impressive historical finds are nothing new in the region. In 2005, for example, excavations at the Dolmen of Menga, a Neolithic monument in nearby Antequera that is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shed light on the site’s ritual uses. A recent study found that the monument was still in use as recently as 1,000 years ago, which may rewrite its history.

If the past is any guide, Málaga’s next great discovery may be just one excavation away.

#6407. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.

A riveting and intimate account of the iconic achievement of Artemis II, Earthrise—written by author John Larsen and based on extensive interviews he conducted with Hansen—is a testament to what can be achieved with unity, teamwork, and a bold belief in humanity’s ability to reach for the stars.

#6405. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#6404. Archaeologists Found a Mass Grave of 8,000 Ancient Frogs. Scientists Finally Know Who Killed Them.

The remains of a yearlong feast had been waiting in a ditch to be found for 1,700 years.

Scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have teamed up to solve the whodunit: 8,000 dead frogs discovered nearly a decade ago in a single ditch in Cambridgeshire, England. The twist? The frogs had been dead for 1,700 years. The scientists have put the mystery to rest by pinning the blame on a group of hungry short-eared owls. Reaching that conclusion, though, doesn’t clear every suspect in the case.

The questions began between 2016 and 2018, when work on the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme uncovered a ditch filled with amphibian bones. Radiocarbon dating by the University of Vienna placed the frogs in the Roman era. Experts then used a new method of analysis to measure the frogs’ arm bones, which showed that most of the frogs died young. They were eaten in the winter of their first year.

After studying the odd cold case, zooarchaeologist Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth and Vicki Ewens, senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, published their findings in Environmental Archaeology. Clarkson first compared the damage on the bones with earlier studies of predation and found that birds of prey had likely eaten the frogs. He named short-eared owls and hen harriers as the most likely suspects.

On-site archaeological evidence added a twist, however: the ditch had filled within a single year. How could so many bones pile up so quickly? The research team found that the waters of the surrounding marshy wetlands, including the ditch in question, were retreating during the Roman period. This created ideal breeding conditions for frogs, and more frogs meant more food for predatory birds.

“We suggest natural and anthropogenic environmental changes to explain why this predation occurred in the Middle Roman period,” the authors wrote.

People also changed the landscape. The valley had been heavily wooded during the Iron Age, but snail, pollen, and charcoal evidence showed major changes by the time of the frog massacre. Over time, farmers had cleared large areas of woodland to make grazing land for livestock. This left the frogs with less cover and drew in short-eared owls, which hunt over open grassland.

“We don’t often get an owl’s-eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” Clarkson said in a statement from the university. “The mystery of these frogs has been solved—a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls.”

The owls may not have dined alone, though. Clarkson called the die-off a “short, intensive predation event” that could have drawn a mix of predators, which also fed on shrews, mice, and voles. “Results showed this was the debris left by a community of predators,” the authors wrote.

Human activity may have helped the predators, too. Although people cut down trees to make room for livestock, the researchers said that both the people and their animals were probably elsewhere during winter. That would have made it easier for the owls to roost near the ditch.

In the university’s statement, Ewens said she had “so many theories” about why such a large collection of frog bones turned up there. Working together to answer the question, she added, shows how research on “even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”

Clarkson agreed. “These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world—what wild animals were getting up to in the past,” he said, “and what life was like for them.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria.

According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus, repeated that story without question.

But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die?

Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery.

"We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones, a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email.

What historians largely agree on is that Cleopatra VII, the last queen of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, took her own life and that she chose a method that left her body composed and dignified.

Physical evidence of Cleopatra's death is elusive. Much of Alexandria's royal quarter now lies underwater, and underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, who has been excavating it, hasn't found the queen's mausoleum, Jones said. Even if Cleopatra's remains surfaced, bones would be unlikely to show evidence of snake venom, she added, noting that forensics is outside her area of expertise.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Divers celebrate as a crane pulls an artifact from the waters at Abu Qir bay in Alexandria, Egypt on Aug. 21, 2025.

The best witness may have been Olympus, Cleopatra's personal physician. "Unfortunately, nothing survives of Olympus' account," Jones said.

What does remain is a story told largely by Cleopatra's enemies. The earliest surviving account is a poem by the Roman poet Horace, whose patron was a close friend of Octavian, said Jane Draycott, a historian at the University of Glasgow. His Ode 1.37, written around the time of her death, celebrates Octavian's victory and already pictures the queen handling serpents — yet it ends with grudging admiration for a woman who refused to be paraded as a trophy.

Following her capture, Cleopatra was held under military guard. By then, she had already tried to end her life twice. Cleopatra had tried to stab herself when Roman soldiers broke into the mausoleum where she had barricaded herself, and she later tried to starve herself, stopping only after Octavian threatened her children.

To Draycott, those attempts leave little doubt that Cleopatra would rather die than live as a captive. "She does not want to be a prisoner; she does not want to be led through the streets of Rome in triumph as a defeated foe," she told Live Science.

In the Greco-Roman world, suicide didn't carry the stigma it later acquired under Christianity, she added. "It was a way of wiping the slate clean, removing any shame, any disgrace from yourself." After the defeat of his remaining forces at Alexandria and hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony was the first of the two lovers to die by suicide.

According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, who based his account on that of Cleopatra's personal physician, Cleopatra visited Antony's tomb, bathed, ate and sent Octavian a sealed letter asking to be buried beside Antony, signaling that she meant to die. Octavian realized what was happening and sent messengers rushing to her, but they arrived too late. They found her dead in her royal regalia, with her attendants Iras and Charmion dying beside her.

A statue depicting Cleopatra's suicide by asp, the most famous of several ancient theories.

Jones has compiled what ancient historians, biographers, geographers and physicians wrote about Cleopatra's death. Every source mentions a snakebite, but several also suggest other possibilities, including a poisonous ointment, poison hidden in a hollow hairpin, and snake venom poured into a wound the queen made by biting herself. Only one of these writers, the geographer Strabo, was alive when Cleopatra died, and the only people in the room with her died, too.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio wrote that the sole clue was a pair of faint pricks on her arm. That doesn't settle much, however. "A cobra bite can appear as two small puncture wounds, but not all cobra bites appear this way and not all double puncture wounds result from snakebites," Jones said.

Jones traces the snake version of the story to Octavian, who was in Alexandria when Cleopatra died. Plutarch reported that an image of Cleopatra with an asp clinging to her was carried in Octavian's triumphal procession in Rome. "Octavian, however, was Cleopatra's enemy and for that reason we may not want to accept his account uncritically," Jones said.

Draycott suggested another possible source of confusion: Snake-shaped jewelry was fashionable in Alexandria at the time, so Romans viewing an effigy of the queen may have mistaken a snake bracelet for a real snake.

Draycott doesn't think one snake could have killed all three women. Jones is less certain. Snakes don't inject the same amount of venom with every bite, and some "dry bites" deliver none at all, Jones said. "On the other hand, I don't think it is impossible, as the body of a cobra contains enough venom to kill multiple people," she added.

The general view among historians, Draycott said, is that Cleopatra took some kind of poison — one that worked quickly and didn't cause seizures or vomiting. The absence of these symptoms is telling: An asp is believed to be what is now known as the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), whose venom causes a slow, agonizing death with respiratory failure.

A young Egyptian cobra (Naja haja) strikes a typical defensive pose in scrubland near Sidi Ifni, Morocco.

Cleopatra likely would have had other means, then. Alexandria was the Mediterranean's center of scientific study, and texts from the period, such as Nicander's "Theriaca," catalog venomous animals, Jones noted. Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, even consulted the pharmacologist Zopyrus about antidotes. Plutarch claimed that Cleopatra personally oversaw experiments that observed the effects of deadly poisons on condemned prisoners.

Still, that claim and other poison stories should be read with caution, Draycott said, because they draw on Roman stereotypes about women. In the Roman view, "manly men will battle with swords," while women, seen as "deceitful and weak" at this time, were thought to kill in secret. "They'll sneak it into your food," Draycott said, summing up the stereotype.

Roman writers were equally suspicious. Poisoning allegations dogged the Hellenistic dynasties of ancient Egypt and the neighboring Seleucid kingdom, as well as Rome's own imperial family. Some were probably true, Draycott said, but others may have been foodborne illnesses or other health conditions people didn't understand.

The method may remain a mystery, but for most historians, the motive doesn't change: Cleopatra chose to die on her own terms.

#6402. The Sanctuary of a Healing God Was Lost for 1,800 Years. Archaeologists May Have Finally Found It.

A century of digs in Epidaurus reveals a sacred site where pilgrims flocked to honor the son of Apollo.

In the second century C.E., a traveler named Pausanias wrote about an open-air sacred precinct featuring statues of Asclepius—the Greek god of healing and the son of Apollo—and his wife, Epione, near the city center of Epidaurus. The only issue: Nobody knew the location. But now, a scholar at the University of Athens thinks there’s enough evidence to claim we’ve solved the 1,800-year-old mystery.

Vassilis Lambrinoudakis of the Department of History and Archaeology of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens pored over hundreds of years of research and concluded that a site in Epidaurus is the statue-filled spot Pausanias described.

Excavations started in Epidaurus in the early 1900s, and since 1974, hundreds of student archaeologists have painstakingly excavated in and around the city. Lambrinoudakis collated the research, noting that not only has he likely found the mystery location, but that cult worship of Asclepius took place at the site for longer than we knew about.

The oldest religious building in Epidaurus—dated to around 600 B.C.E.—features a structure with an underground chamber cut directly into the bedrock, likely part of early healing traditions. In Greek mythology, Asclepius took over his father Apollo’s role as a healer, and Epione was worshiped for her ability to help soothe pain. The ancient structure has a pebble-lined floor, walls coated in dark red plaster, and a circular basin built into the floor accessible by staircase. The bottoms of four amphorae are embedded in the bedrock floor. In the fourth century B.C.E., crews built a new circular building directly to the west, likely a “deliberate continuity of the same chthonic cult of Asclepius,” the university wrote in a translated statement.

Nearby, the teams found a ground-level altar made of limestone blocks that they believe is older than both buildings. Lambrinoudakis said the combination of the finds shows the cult likely dates to the seventh century B.C.E.

The structure served as a key gathering point in Epidaurus. Excavations revealed walls that created a processional route to and from the building, essentially an uncovered passageway for visitors. A large square in the center of the sanctuary features open space in front of the temple, a key functional element of the site.

“It could accommodate the throngs of pilgrims who arrived at the site to take part in the sacrificial offering to Asclepius, which was accompanied by a festive procession,” the university wrote. To the east, an altar and platforms included seating for prominent families who watched the sacrificial rituals.

Beneath Building K, excavators found an earlier structure from the early third century B.C.E. that sat on an unusually sturdy limestone foundation. The Roman building on top of it, which was rebuilt several times between the second and late fourth centuries C.E., has a central courtyard that probably had colonnades on at least three sides. The courtyard also has a gravel floor and a small basin made from reused marble pieces. In the building’s southwest corner, a large hall with a small basin or bath and a round room resembles spaces in other Epidaurus buildings that have been linked to the worship of Egyptian gods.

In the northwest corner of Building K, on a lower level, sits an unusual, nearly intact crypt that opens to the north. Along its west side, reused column pieces from an unknown earlier building form a three-part niche, and gaps in the wall behind it let sunlight stream in at midday. “The overall character of ‘K’ suggests that it may have been the site of a mystical cult, particularly during the late Roman period,” the university said, adding they were unable to define who—or what—the cult worshipped.

In the agora of ancient Epidaurus, just northwest of the city’s small theater, excavators had already uncovered a monumental fourth-century B.C.E. fountain complex. More recently, they found a large walled enclosure right next to it. Inside were small clay offerings that may once have hung from trees, a piece of a clay heating vessel, and a pottery fragment scratched with part of Asclepius’s name.

At the center of the enclosure, a well fed an underground pointed-arch tunnel that carried water to the fountain. Because water was central to the worship of Asclepius, the university says the offerings, the well, and the fountain together identify the site as the long-lost town sanctuary Pausanias described. Excavators also found a larger-than-life marble statue of a woman in the enclosure. Lambrinoudakis thinks it may be the statue of Epione that Pausanias saw, but without an inscription, he can’t be sure.

#6401. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#6398. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

#6396. The 7 Best UPS Battery Backups

Keep your essential devices online and protected from the damaging effects of power outages and surges.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Between a modem, desktop computer, and network-attached storage (NAS), modern computing setups require a reliable power source to function effectively. If you work from home or own a small business, you know that nothing halts your workday and puts you behind like an unexpected power outage. An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) keeps your essential devices temporarily online, which provides a window for you to hit send on that last-minute email.

While a standard power strip or surge protector offers sufficient, albeit basic, protection, a UPS ensures devices are properly shut down and are protected from data loss. Beyond just keeping your devices running, the best UPS battery backups also shield sensitive electronics from potentially damaging power surges and fluctuations throughout the day. Read on to see our recommendations covering a range of needs and budgets.

To find the best uninterruptible power supply, we researched dozens of models from the leading brands in this space. Our selection process focused on several key features, including battery life, automatic voltage regulation (AVR), number of outlets, and other advanced features like power management software. After working from home and testing gear in our home offices for years, we understand the critical need for a reliable power source to keep devices online. Our personal experience and circumstances informed our choices, as we considered the models that could protect devices and provide sufficient battery backup during outages.

The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD offers a whopping 12 outlets, six of which can pull pure sine wave alternating current (AC) power from the battery. The six secondary outlets give you plenty of surge protection and power for non-essential devices, so you have a full power solution for everyday, and plenty of emergency backup power in an outage.

The battery backed outlets are clearly marked, so there’s no confusion. The shape itself also cleverly makes extra room for bulky power bricks in two spots, in case you have a couple of larger plugs.

The CyberPower model contains two USB ports—one USB-A and one USB-C—on its front, and an LCD display gives you detailed information on battery capacity and current load. An alarm sounds when something is wrong with either the device or your setup (like the battery is low or the UPS capacity is overloaded), plus there’s a button to mute the alarm as needed.

The CP1500PFCLCD also supports data line protection, so your devices stay safe from power surges that travel through Ethernet. The cord is a foot shorter than our top pick, but this model provides slightly more output capacity, so it’s worth checking out if you want a ton of outlets.

The Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA provides basic backup on a budget, but it lacks the more advanced features of other options. It has eight outlets total, including four battery-backed outlets to plug in devices like a modem, laptop, or NAS. And with an output of 360 watts, it’s the perfect option for home offices, with space to connect multiple devices simultaneously.

There’s a good amount of space between outlets on the Amazon UPS to easily accommodate two larger power bricks without crowding other nearby outlets. Additionally, it has a user-replaceable battery and supports power management software.

As we said, it lacks more advanced features, including AVR, but it’s still a solid, affordable option.

This CyberPower model offers everything you need in a powerful and reliable UPS. It includes 12 surge-protected outlets, with six of those backed by battery power. This gives you ample space to connect various devices, from your home office setup to more fun devices like your PlayStation 5, smart TV, or gaming desktop. The front of the UPS also features both a USB-A and USB-C port for connecting mobile devices.

An LCD panel displays information about battery and power conditions. If the power goes out, this model’s replaceable battery runs for up to 12 minutes at half load, giving you plenty of time to safely power down. It features simulated AVR, which corrects minor power fluctuations but may not be ideal for sensitive high-end gear.

This APC model features power management software and AVR and comes with an LCD panel, all of which make it another great advanced UPS for home offices and small businesses.

The APC’s power management software boasts several additional features, including the ability to remotely shut down your connected devices during an emergency. This prevents potential corruption or data loss. The device also supports a graceful shutdown feature, which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

The UPS offers both data line and coaxial line safeguards to give you extra peace of mind during power disturbances. An informative LCD screen on the front panel displays crucial information, such as battery capacity, load capacity, the number of power events that have occurred, and any system errors.

For added convenience, the UPS is equipped with both a USB-A and a USB-C port on the front to charge your phone or tablet in the same place as your home office equipment.

Most UPS devices take up a lot of floor or desk space. This one, however, measures approximately 4.1 by 10.8 by 5.5 inches, which is more compact than most for easier integration into your current home office.

Even with its smaller design, this UPS packs a punch with seven total surge-protected outlets, five of which offer battery power. It offers 330 watts of output power—perfectly suitable for a more modest setup.

The UPS automatically switches off from the battery backup when your power comes back on. And when the time comes, you can replace its battery instead of replacing the entire unit.

There are some trade-offs to the more compact design. For instance, more advanced models contain a few more outlets. You also miss out on an LCD screen and AVR. However, these compromises bring the cost down on this space-efficient UPS.

This CyberPower UPS easily integrates into a server setup because of its rack-mounting feature. The design makes it an excellent choice for small businesses that have a data center or server room, keeping the UPS close to the devices it’s protecting. It fits into racks as small as 14 inches in depth.

The device features eight battery-backed outlets and an LCD panel, which displays information on battery and power conditions. The screen also shows alerts about potential issues before they affect your devices.

Like other CyberPower models, this one supports management software for monitoring the UPS remotely. Other features include data line protection and an estimated battery runtime of 10 minutes at half load.

Most UPS models offer limited battery life, even at half load, which isn’t ideal for IT professionals or network administrators. This APC model, however, delivers impressive battery runtime, with up to 23 minutes at half load in the event of an outage. That’s almost double what other top models offer, giving you ample time to save your work and safely shut down your devices.

Beyond excellent battery life, this model comes with a number of advanced features, including cloud-based remote power monitoring, remote diagnostics, and email notifications with recommended actions. It also supports graceful shutdown.

All of these premium features mean this UPS costs more and is noticeably larger than other options on the list. That said, its combination of extended runtime and management features makes it a worthwhile investment, particularly for small businesses that want to protect their hardware and data.

A traditional UPS buys you a few minutes, just enough time to save your work and shut down. If the power's out for hours, you need something bigger. The Anker Solix S2000 is a portable power station that doubles as a UPS: Plug it into the wall, plug your gear into it, and when the power cuts out, it switches to battery power in under 10 milliseconds, fast enough for most home office setups.

And it can keep going for a long time. In our testing, the S2000 ran a refrigerator for just over 24 hours on its 2,010 watt-hours of capacity, and a typical home office draws far less. That's enough to keep a desktop PC and monitor running for several hours, or a modem and router online for more than a day. Its LFP battery is rated for 6,000 cycles before dropping to 80 percent capacity, so it should outlast several lead-acid UPS batteries, and it comes with a five-year warranty.

The trade-off is that it's far pricier than a standard UPS, and at 35.7 pounds, it's not something you'll want to move often. But if you live somewhere with long outages, it's the only pick here that can keep your WiFi running all night.

The UPS you choose should come with enough outlets to accommodate all the devices you need to plug in, with some room for additional devices in the future. Pay attention to the distinction between battery-backed outlets, which offer surge protection and battery power during outages, and surge-protected-only outlets, which, as the name suggests, only offer surge protection.

Every model we write about offers surge protection as a standard feature, even on outlets that don’t offer battery power. Batteries enable a UPS to power your devices once the grid fails. That’s why it’s essential to choose a UPS with enough battery-backed outlets to support the devices you want to keep online.

More advanced UPS models typically offer more outlets (and more that are battery-backed). For example, the more affordable Amazon Basics Standby UPS 600VA has eight outlets, four of which have battery backup, while the more advanced CyberPower CP1500AVRLCD3 has 12 outlets, six of which have battery backup. In addition to AC outlets, some UPS models have USB-A or USB-C ports to connect your smartphone and other devices. These ports easily charge your devices without taking up an outlet.

It’s also important to ensure replacing the battery on the UPS you choose is straightforward and easy. This simplifies maintenance and increases the device’s lifespan. Advanced UPS models typically include battery health monitoring features, so you’ll get a heads up when a battery nears the end of its life.

On average, UPS batteries last three to five years before needing replacement, though this lifespan varies depending on usage. Automatic Voltage Regulation, or AVR, stabilizes inconsistent incoming voltage. It converts fluctuating voltage from the power source into a steady, consistent output for connected devices. This protects sensitive electronics from power irregularities without relying on the UPS battery.

As a bonus, AVR reduces wear and tear on the battery, potentially extending its lifespan. Not all models include this feature, particularly those priced on the lower end.

During an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as eight seconds.

During an outage, a UPS inverter converts the direct current (DC) stored in its battery into the alternating current (AC) that devices expect. Power from the wall doesn’t just switch on and off. Its voltage rises and falls in a smooth, rounded curve called a sine wave, swinging from positive to negative and back 60 times a second.

Pure sine wave models output a smooth wave that closely matches utility power, so your devices run on battery the same way they run on the grid. Some models output a simulated sine wave instead, a stepped signal that switches between positive and negative voltage with brief rests at zero. That output works for basic electronics, but it could cause problems for more sensitive electronics, like audio equipment and desktop PCs.

Desktop PCs are the biggest concern. Most use power supplies with active power factor correction (PFC), a circuit that improves efficiency and helps the unit meet energy standards. On a simulated sine wave, some of these power supplies can shut down unexpectedly or run under extra strain. Most devices without active PFC, including modems and routers, can handle a simulated wave without trouble during a typical short outage.

For a gaming PC, workstation, or home theater system, a pure sine wave UPS is the safer bet. The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD lists sine wave output on battery and is designed for active PFC power supplies. The APC BR1500MS2 lists sine wave output on battery with a transfer time of as little as 8 milliseconds.

Having a display on a UPS may seem like a luxury, but it’s very helpful to have some kind of indicator to give you insight into battery status. Compact and budget models, like the APC BE600M1, typically stick to a few status lights that tell you whether the unit is running on wall power or battery.

An LCD screen shows measurements such as battery charge, how much power your devices are drawing, input and output voltage, and, most importantly, estimated runtime. That last one comes in clutch during an outage, since it tells you exactly how many minutes you have to save your work and shut down.

The CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD's color screen tilts upward, so it's easier to read when the UPS sits on the floor under your desk, and the APC BR1500MS2 keeps a running count of the power events it has handled. And if your UPS lives in a bedroom, check whether you can dim or turn off the backlight. A glowing screen is useful during an outage, but less so at 2 a.m. when you’re trying to sleep.

A cable that’s at least five feet long offers greater flexibility in terms of where you place your UPS. A five-foot-long cable reaches wall outlets that are farther away and positions the UPS conveniently for your devices. You’ll have the freedom to place the UPS in the best spot for your setup, such as under a desk or in a server rack. Remember, a short cable potentially limits where you place the UPS, so it’s always a good idea to go longer, not shorter.

UPS models that support management software give you greater control over the UPS from a phone or computer to remotely shut down connected devices, and some support “graceful shutdown,” which automatically shuts down connected equipment if you’re unable to do it when the connected devices reach a predetermined power level.

Other features worth considering include an LCD display to monitor a UPS’s status, expandable battery capacity, and an audible alarm during power disturbances.

Setting up a UPS is straightforward: Simply plug the UPS into a wall outlet and connect your devices to the UPS. This plug-and-play simplicity means a UPS device is great for anyone, no matter their level of technical know-how. But be aware of the following safety guidelines before powering on a UPS in your home office.

Companies advise against connecting devices like copiers, laser printers, or space heaters to a UPS, as these can overload the device. Instead, use a separate surge protector.

Additionally, never plug a UPS into a surge protector or vice versa. It’s also important to avoid plugging a UPS into an extension cord because this can potentially overload the cord and create a fire hazard. It’s recommended to always plug your UPS directly into a grounded wall outlet. Doing so will ensure your UPS operates safely while providing the best possible protection for your devices.

Finding the right UPS battery backup largely comes down to the total wattage you need to keep your computer up and running while you save and shut down. Speaking broadly, we'd tell you that most home office setups with a desktop PC, monitor, modem, and router should look for a UPS around 600 to 1500 volt-amperes (VA).

To get a more accurate idea of what you specifically need, add up the wattage of all your connected devices, then look for a backup that can handle 120 to 130 percent of that load. That will give you enough time to shut down safely with some wiggle room in case you need to finish a task (or have something urgent come up before you can finish up).

Every system is different, but we'd expect a UPS in the 1000 to 1500VA range to keep your desktop and monitor running for about 15 minutes, which should be long enough to save and safely shut down. A smaller model can probably keep laptop-based setup for a similar amount of time, or power a modem and router for 30 to 45 minutes.

These are all broad estimates, though, and will vary based on what specific gear you're using. We recommend calculating your own power needs to figure out exactly how much time you'll have to shut down in the event of an emergency.

Yes, a UPS backup easily powers a router and modem, and this is one of the most common uses for a small unit. This type of hardware usually consumes only about 10 to 30 watts combined, which is relatively low when compared to computers or TVs. Because of this low draw, even a compact unit would be able to keep your internet running for 30 minutes or more during a power outage.

Brandon Russell is a freelance writer covering gear and technology. He started his journey as a news writer at a small newspaper and later began reviewing smartphones, movies, and video games. In his free time, he enjoys the slower, more intentional experience of using a 35mm film camera and making short videos about movies he grew up watching.

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.
