#6395. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

This story was updated on November 13, 2026, to correct the spelling of Katy Croff Bell's name, and to correct the location of the corals mentioned in the story from the Indian to the Pacific Ocean.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

Nearly 50 years after launch, NASA's Voyager 1 probe will pass the one light-day mark on Nov. 18, a symbolic milestone for the agency's longest-running mission. Scientists reflect on the Voyager program's legacy and what comes next.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe, already the farthest human-made object in space, is about to set another record. On Nov. 18, the spacecraft will be so far from Earth that light, the universe's ultimate speed limit, takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

For researchers who worked on the Voyager program and continue to study its data, the symbolic milestone of being a full light-day from Earth celebrates a mission that continues half a century after it began. Since launching in September 1977, the twin Voyager probes have outlasted many of the engineers who built them, and their flybys of the outer solar system planets remain some of the best close-up observations scientists have of those distant worlds.

"Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are transcending generations," Pascal Lee, a planetary scientist at the SETI Institute who was part of the Voyager 2 team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) during its Neptune flyby in 1989, told Live Science. "Not only is their data relevant, but they themselves are still out there, moving into the unknown."

Here is what the Voyagers have revealed about the solar system and interstellar space, what happens when their power finally runs out, and whether anyone — or anything — might ever intercept the messages from Earth they carry.

A NASA simulation showing where Voyager 1 is relative to the sun and solar system planets.

Voyager 1, cruising through space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), is just shy of 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) from Earth. That's the distance light travels in 24 hours, also known as one light-day. The spacecraft will reach this milestone on Nov. 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. ET, after traveling through space for 49 years, two months and 11 days.

As long as that sounds, "it's still pathetically slow in the grand scheme of things," Lee told Live Science.

If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still.

Scientifically speaking, Voyager 1 hasn't even left its home neighborhood yet. In 2012, the probe traveled beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of plasma blown outward by the sun that shields the planets from incoming cosmic radiation. But it still remains within the sun's gravitational grasp, which extends past the Oort Cloud — a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system. Voyager 1 will need about 300 more years just to reach the cloud's inner edge, and possibly 30,000 years to fly beyond it, according to NASA.

"If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still," Lee said.

On its current path, Voyager 1 will pass within 1.7 light-years of a dim star called Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years, at which point it will be closer to that star than to our own sun. Farther out, the nearest star system to our own, Proxima Centauri, sits about 4.24 light-years away — more than 1,500 times farther than Voyager 1 will be on Nov. 18.

Meanwhile Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, took a different route through the solar system after both probes launched in 1977, in order to swing past Uranus and Neptune after revisiting Jupiter and Saturn. Currently in interstellar space about 13 billion miles (21 million km) from Earth, Voyager 2 will reach its own light-day mark in November 2035, according to NASA.

An illustration of the Voyager probes passing beyond the heliopause, into interstellar space.

Crossing the one-light-day mark doesn't change how NASA communicates with the probe, though it does demand more patience.

NASA talks to the spacecraft using radio signals, which travel at the speed of light. At a distance of one light-day, a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and a reply takes another 24 hours to make the return journey.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a recent statement.

As the spacecraft continues to cruise deeper into space, that wait will grow longer. Moreover, 50 years of traversing the solar system and the increasing distance from our sun takes a toll on the probe itself. Because sunlight in the outer reaches is far too faint for solar panels, Voyager 1 relies on nuclear batteries that convert heat from the natural decay of plutonium into electricity. That supply is gradually dwindling, prompting NASA to gradually shut down nonessential instruments to conserve what energy remains and extend the mission as much as possible.

Kelly Perry, a data systems engineer on the Voyager program at JPL, told Live Science via email that the mission team's priority remains the same: "keep the spacecraft going as long as possible."

A montage of planets imaged by the twin Voyager probes, showing Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Before the Voyagers launched, the outer solar system was largely a blur of telescopic speculation. The twin probes took advantage of a planetary alignment that comes around only once every 176 years, using the gravity of giant planets to slingshot themselves onward.

Together, they have discovered 23 moons across the outer solar system, revealed faint rings around Jupiter and captured the first detailed atmospheric profiles of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They also gave the first detailed, close-up views of Jupiter's moon Europa, transforming our perception of it from a blurry speck into a remarkably smooth, geologically young world — and now one of the prime candidates for finding extraterrestrial life.

We had no idea what they looked like. And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places.

Among the more striking finds, Voyager 1 spotted active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io in 1979, the first time they had been seen on any world other than Earth.

"We had no idea what they looked like," Lee said. "And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places," he added.

"That's what Voyager was for me — a voyage of discovery," he said.

These discoveries laid the groundwork for decades of follow-up exploration, including NASA's Galileo mission to Jupiter and the Cassini mission to Saturn. Decades later, as the only spacecraft to return in situ data from outside the heliosphere, the probes also proved that interstellar space is a dynamic, complex frontier rather than an empty vacuum.

Each Voyager spacecraft launched with 10 science instruments. Today, only two remain active on Voyager 1 and three on Voyager 2, measuring the magnetic fields, plasma and cosmic rays of interstellar space.

NASA began switching off the others one by one decades ago to conserve power, including the camera on Voyager 1 just minutes after it snapped the famous "Pale Blue Dot" portrait of the solar system in 1990. Ongoing power-saving reconfigurations have since helped keep the aging spacecraft operational nearly 50 years into its lifetime.

Voyager's iconic "Pale Blue Dot" image shows Earth as a "mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam," in the words of Carl Sagan.

In one such recent effort, nicknamed the "Big Bang," engineers shut off certain high-power subsystems while switching on lower-power alternatives, which "bought us almost two more years during which we will not need to turn any instrument off," Perry said.

With onboard power steadily dwindling, however, "there's a recognition that it won't be forever," Deana Weibel, an anthropologist at the Grand Valley State University in Michigan who co-authored an upcoming book about the Golden Record aboard the Voyager probes, told Live Science.

Because Voyager is a science mission, its mission will be considered finished when "no science instruments are operational," Perry said. "The Science Team decided that the last remaining instrument will be the magnetometer," she added. "We will never intentionally power off this instrument."

After the science data eventually stops, both probes may still keep beaming back basic engineering updates, such as about their health and power status, until around 2036, according to NASA. Even after the spacecraft finally fall silent, they will keep coasting through interstellar space, and "analysis shows that they should remain intact," Perry said.

Scientists will still be able to calculate their positions based on their last known speed and trajectories, Weibel said. "We'll know intellectually where it is unless it gets intercepted."

An illustration of Voyager shown next to the Golden Record.

Theoretically, yes. But interstellar space is so unfathomably vast that the chances of aliens finding the probes are vanishingly small, Lee said.

That makes it unlikely that aliens will ever find the Voyager Golden Records — twin gold-plated discs meant to portray the diversity of life on Earth. They hold sounds such as wind and animal calls, greetings in 55 languages, images of our planet and a celestial map pinpointing its location — all intended for a hypothetical civilization capable of retrieving and playing them. (The probes also carry visual instructions for spinning the records).

In that sense, the Golden Records are as much an artistic exercise as a scientific one.

"The chances of us going after Voyager 1 and bringing it back for the Smithsonian — not that it's likely — are more believable than any chance of an alien civilization finding it, and then playing the record," Lee said.

Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort

If an extraterrestrial civilization did find the probe after we lost contact with it, "we would have no way of knowing," Weibel added. "It becomes something that's powered entirely by imagination at that point."

So why send a message at all? All three scientists interviewed for this story see the Golden Record as a cosmic time capsule, a symbolic gesture meant to unite humanity around a shared home planet. For all its imperfections, including the omission of some widely spoken languages and a few mislabeled tracks, the disc remains an enduring emblem of human presence on Earth, they said.

"Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort," Perry told Live Science. "Although I won't be able to speak to the Voyager spacecraft any more, I love knowing that I'll always be able to look to the stars and know they're still on their way."

#6393. Earth’s early crust left a fingerprint in rocks for a billion years, then it vanished

Lead in ancient rocks may help pinpoint when modern plate tectonics took hold and began reshaping how Earth recycles its crust.

Earth’s surface is made of plates that slide, collide, and sink back into the planet, and it’s tempting to assume it has always worked that way. Rocks older than about 2.6 billion years carry a chemical signature that says otherwise.

The signature comes from a pool of crust that formed roughly 4 billion years ago and kept getting remelted in place for more than a billion years.

Between about 2.75 and 2.63 billion years ago, the pattern changes sharply. One source’s signature vanishes from the record, and the other turns up only rarely after that.

The researchers interpret the shift as a possible sign that modern plate tectonics was taking hold and reshaping how Earth recycled its crust.

The study is an interpretation of a global compilation of lead measurements, and the authors call their explanation a testable hypothesis rather than a settled fact.

Janne Liebmann of Curtin University in Perth, Australia, led the work with colleagues at Curtin’s School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and Queen’s University in Canada.

“New crust often forms by melting older rock, leaving behind a distinctive chemical fingerprint,” Liebmann said.

The fingerprint is carried by lead. Uranium and thorium decay into three different forms of lead at three different rates. So the mix of lead in a rock records how much uranium and thorium its source held, and for how long.

Some minerals, including feldspar and certain sulphides, take in lead as they crystallize but almost no uranium or thorium. Their lead mix is fixed at the moment they form, which makes them a record of the magma they grew from.

The team compiled published lead measurements on such minerals from rocks whose ages were known independently. They added eight new feldspar analyses from China, West Africa, and Finland.

After discarding samples whose lead had been disturbed, 1,235 remained, with ages from 3.8 billion years to the present.

In rocks older than about 2.6 billion years, the lead points to two sources that split from the mantle between 4.0 and 3.7 billion years ago. One was rich in uranium relative to lead, the other poor.

Both show up in rocks from ancient continental cores around the world.

For those signatures to develop, the two sources had to stay chemically isolated for at least a billion years.

The authors’ explanation is a primitive crust split into an upper layer and a lower layer, each with its own uranium budget, that magmas kept tapping without destroying.

Most of the old rocks in the dataset are granites, which can form when existing crust melts. That fits the idea that early Earth repeatedly reworked its crust in place.

After about 2.6 billion years ago, the lead in new rocks clusters near the average for the whole planet. The spread in the inferred uranium budgets of their sources roughly halves.

A statistical test for abrupt changes, repeated 300 times on reshuffled versions of the data, kept finding the same break between 2.75 and 2.63 billion years ago.

The break held in the full dataset and in two subsets the team checked separately. Australian samples make up 71% of the compilation, so the authors treated the 358 non-Australian samples as an independent test. The break appeared there too.

The uranium-rich source never reappears. The uranium-poor one surfaces only four times afterward, in granites from Russia and Australia between 1.6 billion and 400 million years ago.

Liebmann’s team wrote that the old sources were either destroyed, most likely by being dragged back into the mantle, or cut off from the places where new crust was made.

Both fit a planet that had begun moving crust around and recycling it, with magma production shifting from the interiors of plates to their edges.

Other changes geologists have documented in rocks of that age line up with the break. Continents were becoming thicker and richer in silica. Buried rocks began recording sharper contrasts in temperature. And what may have been the first supercontinent was assembling.

“It marks the transition from an early Earth where ancient crust could be repeatedly melted and reworked in place, to a system capable of moving and recycling crust on a much larger scale,” said co-author Chris Kirkland of Curtin.

Kirkland said the finding helps explain when Earth developed the global system of moving plates that distinguishes it from Venus and Mars.

Lead isotopes record that the old sources stopped feeding new magma. They don’t by themselves show plates sinking.

The team wrote that direct evidence for global subduction at that time is limited, and that its model is a framework still to be tested.

The dataset also leans on Australia, where recent mapping projects have produced far more lead measurements than elsewhere.

The non-Australian check helps, but a more even global sample would test the result harder.

One detail may prove useful. The rare reappearances of the uranium-poor source suggest pieces of that ancient lower crust still survive under some continents.

If so, they could account for part of a long-standing puzzle. Surface rocks on average hold more uranium-derived lead than the whole Earth should, which implies a hidden, uranium-poor reservoir somewhere below.

The team’s data are available through the EarthBank platform, where other researchers could test the break against new samples as they are measured.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A.

#6392. When AI runs the lab, who checks the results?

A review across 11 fields examines how scientists test AI-generated results as machines take on more of the work of proposing and running experiments.

It’s easy to picture AI in science as a very fast assistant: feed it the data and it finds the pattern. A review by researchers at 94 institutions calls that picture out of date.

Some AI systems now take on several steps in the research process, from reading papers and proposing hypotheses to directing robots in the lab and adjusting experiments based on the results.

The authors ask how much of what comes out of that loop can be trusted. They rank the field’s claims by how well each has been tested in the real world.

The review is a survey of published work across 11 fields, not a new experiment.

The lead authors include Yongjun Xu of the Institute of Computing Technology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Heyang Li of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Co-authors come from institutions including the University of Queensland and Berlin’s Hertie School.

The authors’ own 2021 review, in the same journal, described AI as a powerful tool for analyzing data. AlphaFold, which predicts a protein’s shape from its sequence, was the model case.

That program answered one question that had resisted decades of work and left the rest of the job to people.

Five years on, the review describes systems built from six modules that feed each other.

One reads papers, one analyzes data, one proposes hypotheses, one runs experiments, one writes the report, and one adjusts the whole process based on what failed.

Large language models supply the knowledge and reasoning, software agents sequence the work, and robots supply the hands.

Some groups, the authors wrote, are already testing whether AI can take part in peer review itself.

The clearest example comes from materials science. An autonomous laboratory called A-Lab was handed 58 target compounds.

Drawing synthesis recipes from the literature and adjusting when a route failed, it made 41 of them in 17 days.

The review treats materials science as the field where the loop is most complete, with generative models proposing new crystals and robotic platforms making and testing them.

Other fields are further behind. In medicine, the authors flagged limited prospective validation and the risk of fabricated outputs.

In geoscience, models trained on past conditions struggle when the conditions themselves shift.

The review’s most practical contribution is a grading scheme. For each field, the authors coded the level of validation behind AI results on a scale from A to D.

An A means a method has been experimentally validated or is already deployed in real workflows. A B means a prototype tested in a controlled, closed-loop setting.

A C means the result rests on benchmarks, simulations, or retrospective tests. A D means the work is still conceptual.

The point, the authors wrote, is that a high score on a benchmark is not the same as a discovery.

Closing what they call the reality gap between benchmark success and real-world use is, in their words, a top priority.

Three constraints recur across every field in the review. Standardized, high-quality data remain scarce.

Deep networks still trade interpretability for accuracy, so a model can predict a molecule’s behavior without explaining it.

And generative models can produce outputs that look plausible while violating physical laws, which the authors tie to the lack of explicit physical constraints in current architectures.

A fourth limit is human. The review cites earlier warnings that AI’s fluency can create what one group called “illusions of understanding,” with scientists mistaking output for insight and converging on the same few methods.

The authors also put a price on scale. Global data centers used about 415 terawatt-hours of electricity during 2024.

The review projects that figure roughly doubling by 2030, an increase about equal to Japan’s current annual consumption.

For science, the authors wrote, the cost of discovery is becoming tied to electricity prices and hardware supply.

In the United States, about 56% of data center electricity comes from fossil fuels. The authors put the resulting emissions at more than 105 million tons of carbon dioxide a year.

Training a single large model, they wrote, can cost from thousands to hundreds of millions of dollars, which risks a “computational divide” between well-funded labs and everyone else.

A review maps what has been published, and the authors are candid that maturity is uneven and that the grades are theirs. The open question for any one field is the A-to-D test itself: has anyone checked the machine’s result against the world?

The authors expect the next decade to be the test. Governments in the United States, Britain, the European Union, and China have all launched AI-for-science strategies.

The review’s case is that the advantage will go to whoever best combines data, computing, and people, not to the biggest budget.

The authors’ closing line is a limit as much as a forecast. AI, they wrote, will serve as a cognitive copilot rather than a replacement for scientists.

The review was published in the journal The Innovation.

An unusual pair of seated figurines was discovered in a Stone Age grave in Romania in the 1950s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two Stone Age figurines ‪—‬ the Thinker and the Seated Woman ‪—‬ were discovered in a prehistoric cemetery in Romania.

In 1956, archaeologists unearthed two unique figurines from one grave while excavating a Stone Age cemetery in southeast Romania. The unusual figurines — known as the Thinkers of Cernavodă or the Thinker and the Seated Woman — were made by people from the Hamangia culture and may be linked to ancient astronomical beliefs.

The Thinkers of Cernavodă are in the collection of the National Museum of Romanian History and are a key part of the country's cultural heritage. They were crafted from fired clay and measure about 4.5 inches (11.5 centimeters) tall. The two figurines may represent a man (the Thinker) and a woman (the Seated Woman), according to the museum.

The Thinker sits on a low, four-legged stool. He bends forward slightly, rounding his back and neck, and his arms are bent. He rests his elbows on his knees and his head in his hands. This pose gives him a meditative quality, according to the museum, which is why he has been named after Auguste Rodin's famous 1904 bronze sculpture. The Seated Woman also has a long, bent neck and a small face. She has prominent hips, thighs and breasts. Her right leg is bent, and her hands rest on her knee.

The figurines are about 7,000 years old and were made by the Hamangia people, a Late Neolithic culture that stretched from the Danube River to the Black Sea. According to archaeologist Dumitru Berciu, who excavated the Cernavodă cemetery, the Hamangia culture lasted from about 5200 to 4500 B.C. The people focused primarily on sheep and goat herding, and they built defensive hilltop settlements. They also crafted spiral-decorated pottery and human-shaped figurines. But while Berciu found dozens of male and female figurines in the Cernavodă cemetery, he noted that both Thinkers were unusual for being depicted seated rather than standing.

The specific meaning of the Thinkers is unclear. Berciu suggested that the figurines were somewhat stylized, rather than realistic, because they served a magical or religious purpose. Since solar worship was common among later Bronze Age groups in Europe — as evidenced by artifacts like the Nebra sky disc from Germany and an ornate sun chariot from Denmark — Berciu interpreted the figurines as possibly connected to sun worship.

But the National Museum of Romanian History has suggested that the two figurines may have been made specifically as a pair, representing the complementary principles of masculine and feminine natures or a Neolithic family unit. Another interpretation is that the sculptures depict a pair of mourners who were buried with the deceased.

While the original meaning of the 7,000-year-old sculptures remains a mystery, people continue to be drawn to the contemplative pair, and the male Thinker figures prominently today in the logo of the National Museum of Romanian History.

#6388. Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Taking gender-affirming hormone therapy was the right decision for 97 percent surveyed

Demonstrators rally at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025 in support of gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. The vast majority of transgender and gender diverse young people are satisfied with their decision to take hormone therapy, according the largest survey on the topic.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

#6387. Córdoba’s famous orange trees face a test in one of Spain’s hottest cities

Olive and holm oak leaves kept working at temperatures that damaged orange and tipu, a 17-species test finds, a guide to heat-tolerant trees.

Orange trees line the streets and plazas of Córdoba, in southern Spain, and a tree from a warm climate seems like a safe bet for a hot city.

In a test of 17 common street and park trees in Córdoba, the orange was among the first to fail in the heat.

The orange tree’s leaves had lost 90% of their photosynthetic function by the time they reached 123°F (50.6°C). Olive leaves held on to 141°F (60.6°C), and holm oak kept working longer than any other species at the halfway mark.

Native Mediterranean and temperate trees tolerated more heat than exotic species from the subtropics, the study found.

The trees were sampled during one week in one city, so the rankings are a starting point rather than a verdict.

Sonia Vega-Rosete and Cristina Bastias of the University of Córdoba ran the test.

Córdoba’s summers already pass 104°F (40°C) on more than 15 days in some months, according to records from AEMET, Spain’s weather agency, and the count is rising.

Street trees cool a city with shade and with the water their leaves release. If heat damages the leaves, both services shrink.

The researchers picked 17 species that are common in Córdoba and span a range of origins. The native Mediterranean trees included olive, holm oak, cork oak and carob.

Ash, white poplar and elm stood in for native temperate trees. The exotics from the subtropics included orange, jacaranda, chinaberry, tipu and catalpa.

In the last week of June 2025, the team cut one sun-exposed branch from each of five mature trees per species, all growing in irrigated city parks.

Back in the lab, they punched leaf discs about 0.6 inches (1.5 centimeters) across and sealed them in bags.

The bags went into a water bath for 30 minutes at each of 11 temperatures, from 77°F to 140°F (25°C to 60°C), six discs per temperature.

Afterward the team measured how well each disc’s light-harvesting machinery still worked.

From those readings, they fitted a curve for each species and read off three thresholds.

The first was the temperature where damage began, and the other two were where half and 90% of function was gone.

Every species held up to about 108°F (42.5°C). Above that, the damage threshold ranged from 108°F for tipu to 125°F (51.5°C) for holm oak.

The halfway point separated the groups most clearly. Native species lost half their function at an average of about 125°F (51.5°C), exotics at about 121°F (49.6°C).

The gap between the two groups was unlikely to be chance.

For 90% loss, the averages were about 135°F (57.2°C) for natives and 130°F (54.4°C) for exotics.

Grouped by climate of origin, Mediterranean and temperate trees reached about 136°F and 134°F (57.6°C and 56.4°C) before losing 90% of function, and subtropical trees about 128°F (53.5°C).

Whether a tree keeps its leaves in winter made no difference. Evergreen and deciduous species were spread across the rankings.

“This allowed us to identify the temperature thresholds at which the photosynthetic performance of these species begins to be impaired, which could compromise their ability to ‘cool their surroundings,'” Vega-Rosete said.

The orange tree, chinaberry, catalpa and tipu are planted across Córdoba’s parks and streets, often for their looks or their history there. All four were among the least heat-tolerant trees.

The authors offer one explanation. A subtropical climate pairs warmth with humidity and plenty of water, and Córdoba supplies the warmth without the other two.

To measure that gap, the team mapped each species’ home climate from occurrence records in GBIF and other databases, matched to climate data from WorldClim.

For the subtropical species, the farther Córdoba’s climate was from the climate of their native range, the lower the temperature at which leaf damage began. Native species showed no such drop.

Holm oak, whose native range includes places as hot as Córdoba, had the highest damage threshold of all.

Leaf temperatures matter here. The authors note that leaves can run 14°F to 18°F (8°C to 10°C) hotter than the air around them, and up to 36°F (20°C) hotter in full sun.

A 104°F afternoon can put a leaf past the damage threshold of several of these trees.

The heat-tolerant trees shared a build. Their wood was denser, their leaves were thicker, and each leaf packed more dry matter into its area.

Species with heavier leaves per unit area lost half their function at higher temperatures, and species with denser wood resisted the onset of damage longer.

Such traits were most pronounced in the native Mediterranean evergreens.

The subtropical exotics, and a few temperate trees such as white poplar and black locust, had the opposite build: bigger leaves with more nitrogen, geared to fast growth.

All of the trees grew in watered parks, so the thresholds may differ for trees on dry streets or in other cities.

The leaves came from a single week of a hot summer. The five trees of each species were pooled, so the test gives one curve per species rather than a range.

The thresholds also capture only one part of how a tree copes with heat. Heat-shock proteins and other chemical defenses weren’t part of the study.

The authors wrote that the same test needs to run in other cities, climates, seasons and years, and on more species, before the rankings can guide planting broadly.

The full study was published in the journal Urban Forestry & Urban Greening.

#6386. Exercise may have an overlooked social benefit beyond boosting your mood

Mice with running wheels fought less over food and warmth, suggesting that exercise can influence their social behavior.

Exercise is usually recommended for the heart, the lungs, and a better mood. In mice, a new study suggests that it may also alter how animals treat one another.

Less fighting over food and a warm resting place was observed in mouse pairs housed with a working running wheel.

Pairs whose wheel had been locked fought more often. Greater activity was also recorded in brain areas tied to social behavior among the mice that ran.

The work was led by Liz Kirby of Ohio State University. She is an associate professor of behavioral neuroscience in the Department of Psychology.

The findings come from mice and were presented at a scientific meeting. They have not yet appeared in a journal.

“Mice are known to be naturally social. They like hanging out with other mice, just like humans like hanging out with other humans,” Kirby said.

“They also exercise naturally. If you give them a running wheel, they run about six miles a night, voluntarily.”

Mice were housed in pairs for six weeks by Kirby’s team. Each pair consisted of two males or two females.

A running wheel was available to some pairs at any hour of the day or night. Other pairs were given a wheel that could not turn.

The same object was therefore present in every cage, yet only one group could run on it.

Each pair was then given something to compete for. A tasty treat was used in one test. In another, the prize was a warm resting spot with room for only one mouse.

The researchers recorded behaviors linked to competitive fighting. These included attempts to steal the food or to push a cage mate off the warm spot.

According to Kirby, a food pellet was shared more readily by the mice with working wheels. Mice with locked wheels were not as good at sharing it.

“They would rip it from each other’s paws and run away with it in a cage and chase each other down. Generally very rude behavior when it comes to mealtime,” Kirby said.

A follow-up experiment limited some mice to scheduled wheel sessions. These sessions lasted six hours a day and were held five days a week. Kirby called them visiting the gym.

The same tests were carried out after six weeks on that schedule. Kirby said that living with a wheel and visiting the gym both seemed to reduce fighting over limited resources.

Constant access to a wheel therefore did not appear necessary for the mice to fight less.

Will Butke is a doctoral student in Kirby’s lab and the lead author of the study. The effects of running inside the brain were also examined by him and his colleagues.

A technique that marks recently active brain cells was used. Some regions linked to social behavior were more active in the mice that ran. Other regions remained unchanged.

“This points toward the idea that this isn’t just a brain-wide increase in activation, but instead that the activation is specifically in certain subregions of the brain,” Butke said.

These measurements indicate which areas were more active in the running mice. They cannot show whether that activity explains the reduced fighting.

Clubs where people exercise together have grown quickly. The fitness app Strava reported that new clubs on its platform nearly quadrupled in 2025.

The total was put at 1 million clubs by Strava. Hiking clubs grew fastest and were followed by running clubs.

Meanwhile, loneliness has worried health officials.

Falling rates of social connection were described as “an urgent public health concern” in a 2023 advisory. It was issued by U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy.

According to Butke, research on what happens in the brain when people exercise socially is limited.

“People like to run in groups or exercise together – not only because you get to have a person you can rely upon, but also it gets you into a social context where you can de-stress,” he said.

Mice and people are difficult to compare directly. Even so, Kirby said the work suggests that exercise has a direct social benefit, since competitive fighting was reduced.

“This adds to the list of potential benefits you could be getting by exercising,” Kirby said.

“It’s not just going to make your heart healthier, and it’s not just going to reduce your risk for cancer, obesity and stroke, but it also might help strengthen your social ties.”

A poster is an early step, and a full paper has not yet been released. The number of mice tested and the brain regions that changed would be detailed in that paper.

All of the mice lived in pairs, so the results describe exercise with a companion nearby. The behavior of a mouse that runs alone remains a separate question.

Future research could test whether exercise changes how people share and compete, as it did in these mice.

The work was presented on November 18 as a poster at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

#6385. From Noah’s Ark to Oak Island: In 1976, We Named the 7 Great Quests of Man. Bigfoot Still Hasn’t Called Back

Some quests got closer. One got debunked. And one may owe its modern revival to this very magazine.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

“A quest is a search and an adventure,” reads the opening salvo of the September 1976 Popular Mechanics cover story, “7 Great Quests of Man.” Admittedly, this is a somewhat muted, almost “Maid of Honor Reads the Webster’s Dictionary Definition of Love for Her Toast”-esque opener to place beneath such a grandiose headline.

In defense of that half-century-old article, finding a really great opening line for a story can be hard. That’s as true now as it was 50 years ago. At least the author didn’t take the easy way out and just start it by quoting somebody else instead.

But what of the “Great Quests” themselves? Have any of them been conquered in the last half-century? Have any of the tools and technologies developed since 1976 brought us a smidge closer to solving these age-old mysteries?

To mark the 50th anniversary of the “7 Great Quests of Man,” we took a look back at the quests that captivated readers in 1976, and how close we’ve come to bringing them to an end since then.

The first Great Quest on the list is one of the oldest, the search for the lost continent of Atlantis. The earliest extant record of the story of Atlantis was penned by Plato, who put the words in the mouth of his interlocutor Critias in a pair of dialogues written around 360 B.C.E.

By 1976, Atlantis was having a moment in the sun (one whose rays could presumably reach its watery depths). Paranormal phenomena researcher Charles Berlitz’s book The Mystery of Atlantis was back on bookshelves in a new paperback edition, and on television, everyone from Leonard Nimoy to Jabberjaw was seemingly in search of the sunken continent.

In “7 Great Quests of Man,” after dismissing the claims of a psychic who said Atlantis would rise again, we actually offered up a different theory: that Atlantis had already been found back in the 1960s, and it was actually a volcanic island called Santorini.

At the time, we dated the eruption to sometime between 1480 and 1450 B.C.E. Modern radiocarbon evidence suggests it happened more than a century earlier, likely around 1600 B.C.E. Either way, the blast caused a large part of the island to sink, leaving only three smaller islands above water (including the largest, now called Thera or Santorini).

“During the 1960s excavations of Thera revealed that it had once been the home of the Minoans,” we wrote, “These were a highly civilized, seafaring people whose center was on the island of Crete about 70 miles from Santorini. The Minoans on Thera had been wiped out by the eruption. The well-preserved ruins now being uncovered are one of the major archaeological finds of this century.”

Here in the 21st century, Santorini is actually still making waves, literally. We reported last year that magma from the island’s crust caused a remarkable 25,000 tremors in just a 30-day period. And while advancements in tech like sonar have yet to turn up any evidence of Atlantis, intrepid adventurers have uncovered several other sunken cities, from the relics of Canopus and the Sanctuary of Poseidon at Samikon to the medieval city of Shipden and the “Atlantis of the Sands,” Ubar.

Next up on the list was Noah’s Ark. That readers in 1976 were dying to know where Noah’s Ark was is actually no surprise; it would be the same as folks in 2026 wanting to find the Trojan Horse after seeing The Odyssey. That’s because in 1976, a documentary called In Search of Noah’s Ark proved a box-office sensation, becoming one of the top ten highest-grossing films of the year.

Part of the film’s appeal was the sentiment that the remnants of the Biblical vessel could well be hidden away on Turkey’s Mount Ararat, and only the political strife of our modern times was keeping us from finding the ancient treasure. After all, during this time, the United States had actually implemented an arms embargo on Turkey after its actions in Cyprus in 1974, so things were undoubtedly fraught geopolitically in the region.

“7 Great Quests of Man” suggests as much. “Currently the Turkish government is discouraging foreign expeditions to Mount Ararat,” it concludes, “it’s in a politically sensitive area.” Back then, we said that Ark hunters would no doubt return to the site “as soon as restrictions are lifted,” which is the kind of thing you casually say when you don’t realize there’s about to be a violent military coup in four years.

Now, in the 21st century, some progress has actually been made in the search for Noah’s Ark. In October 2026, we reported that soil samples were taken from Mount Ararat’s Durupinar formation, a peculiar geological feature in the area that’s long been considered a potential resting place for the Biblical vessel. The preliminary tests showed a high concentration of organic material, such as wood. Further lab work is being undertaken to try and determine “if man-made activity or decaying wood sit in the soil.”

“The hottest quest going in 1976 is the quest for the Loch Ness monster,” we wrote in “7 Great Quests of Man,” and that was no joke. 1976 really was Nessie’s year, with coverage of the alleged cryptid even appearing in the pages of the MIT Technology Review and the New York Times.

Why was the Loch Ness Monster having such a moment during the Bicentennial? Simple: In 1975, new photographs purportedly showing the creature had surfaced. While we’re all familiar with the famous 1930s photo of Nessie’s alleged neck rising above the water, the two new pictures came courtesy of an underwater camera, and seemed to show the creature close up and beneath the waves. “One shows a close-up of what may be the head of an unknown animal,” we wrote in 1976, “the other what may be its head, neck and body.”

Back then, we cited numerous notable biologists who felt the images were “sufficiently suggestive of a large aquatic animal” and concluded that “the long search may be nearing a conclusion.”

Back in 2013, Scientific American blamed the photos’ appeal on pareidolia, our brain’s habit of finding faces and figures where there are none. The photo that was thought to show Nessie’s head “is most likely a gnarly tree-stump on the loch floor.”

That being said, the last few years have still yielded some interesting Loch Ness Monster talk, from a 2025 study concluding that Nessie wouldn’t look like you think (if it exists at all) to the recent recovery of a 1970s Loch Ness Monster trap with its own underwater camera (which captured no Nessie pictures, unfortunately).

So, in a sense, the Loch Ness Monster mystery is kind of like the Starland Vocal Band’s “Afternoon Delight.” It’s still around on the periphery today, and we’re all a little confused as to why it was such a big thing back in ’76.

2) Could Bigfoot beat the Six Million Dollar Man in a fight?

And in 1976, one of those questions was finally answered. In a two-part episode of The Six Million Dollar Man called “The Secret of Bigfoot,” Steve Austin (the character played by Lee Majors, not the professional wrestler) faced off against Bigfoot (played by André the Giant, the actual professional wrestler). Believe it or not, this was just one small component of the Bigfoot craze that overtook America in the 1970s. There were Bigfoot movies, Bigfoot TV shows, a Bigfoot board game and, unbeknownst to the average American, the FBI was even actively investigating the legitimacy of hairs that reportedly came from Sasquatch himself.

For real, Bigfoot has an FBI file, and we read it.

As our article pointed out back then, while talk of Yetis and Sasquatches originated near the start of the 20th century, 1970s Bigfoot mania was ignited by the famed Patterson-Gimlin film. You know the one. You’ve undoubtedly seen it. Back in 1967, amateur monster hunters Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin went out into the woods with a camera and captured footage of a seven-foot-tall creature covered in hair strolling by. While some were skeptical of the footage, thinking it was just a guy in a suit, back in 1976 our writer spoke to a primate expert at the Smithsonian Institution who said, “I could not see the zipper and I still can’t.”

Now in 2026, though, you can see the zipper if you want—in a manner of speaking, anyway.

We don’t want to bum out the Bigfoot believers here. Look, maybe there is still a Sasquatch out there somewhere—and if you ask that one guy, there certainly was one, but it’s dead now). But as for the Patterson-Gimlin film? That received a thorough debunking in 2026 thanks to the revelatory documentary Capturing Bigfoot. The film, which debuted at SXSW in March 2026, confirms that the famous footage was a hoax, revealing never-before-seen “rehearsal footage” shot by the men in 1966, featuring a different design for the Sasquatch.

“Oak Island, a small island on Mahone Bay off the coast of Nova Scotia, is the site of what has to be the most frustrating quest of modern times,” we wrote back in 1976. “There may be a treasure on the island. People have known where the treasure is buried for nearly 200 years. But it is so cleverly protected that all attempts to recover it have been foiled.”

From the supposed “Money Pit” to the cipher stone to the Oak Island Curse, this north-of-the-border treasure hunt has built up its own glossary of lore and lingo over the last two centuries as eager treasure hunters braved booby traps in search of a historic payday. Popular Mechanics first covered the Oak Island treasure hunt 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures,” and its allure attracted the attention of major names like John Wayne and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Here in 2026, we can say that the Oak Island mystery stands out from the other “Great Quests” outlined in our pages 50 years ago for one specific reason: the “7 Great Quests of Man” list itself had a direct influence on the current-day search for answers about Oak Island.

How do we know that? Well, the new faces of the Oak Island treasure hunt said so themselves.

“Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” Marty Lagina told us. “There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” brother Rick Lagina chimed in. “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.” The two men are the stars of the long-running television series The Curse of Oak Island, currently airing its 14th season. While they’ve yet to uncover some massive trove at the bottom of the much-discussed Money Pit, the show’s efforts have helped uncover some of the island’s previously undocumented history, and the series’ popularity has kept the mysterious island in the cultural zeitgeist.

“Did visitors from other planets come to earth in ancient times?” we asked in 1976. Then we answered: “Recently, yes has become a very popular answer to that question.” And this was no exaggeration. People really were all in on this theory in the 1970s, and not just the fringe conspiracy crowd.

To give you an idea of just how pervasive alien fever was, we need to touch on a film called Chariots of the Gods. Based on the pseudoscientific work of Erich von Däniken, this 1970 documentary laid out the theory that the world’s religions and early human development were all influenced by ancient extraterrestrial visitors.

How did audiences in the Disco Decade receive this claim? Well, not only was the film a commercial success, it actually managed to get an Academy Award nomination for Best Documentary Feature that year, putting it up alongside the historic concert film Woodstock and the MLK documentary King: A Filmed Record... Montgomery to Memphis. That would be like if this year You Can See Everything had to compete against an episode of Ancient Aliens at the Oscars.

Supporters of the theory pointed to ancient constructions they felt couldn’t have been built with “primitive tools,” and massive monuments constructed that could only be seen properly from the skies. Skeptics claimed these “view-from-above” tributes were intended for gods in the heavens, but true believers said it was a message to aliens.

In our world today, the ancient alien theory still gets bandied about from time to time. Recently, we’ve covered phenomena like the “Black Knight” satellite and the Silurian hypothesis, both of which have attracted their fair share of fringe “it was aliens” theories. But arguably the greatest cultural cachet the conspiracy theory has today is the face we’re all picturing when we read the sentence “it was aliens.”

You know who we’re talking about. You’ve seen the memes.

Author Giorgio Tsoukalos got the meme treatment all the way back in 2010 for his credulous role on the immensely popular television show Ancient Aliens. That series, which still airs today, took the torch of Chariots of the Gods and ran with it, keeping the “ancient aliens” theory in the popular discourse through 22 television seasons, a video game, and even an adjacent series in which audiences watch very stoned people watch the show. As a Great Quest, we’ve come no closer to finding proof of ancient aliens, but as a pop culture concept? The brand has literally never been stronger.

“Ask most scientists what they think of the ancient-astronaut theories, and they will just snort at you,” we wrote in 1976. “But that doesn’t mean that they don’t take the subject of intelligent life in space seriously. They do. They are now trying to contact extraterrestrial civilizations. That is the last, and perhaps the most exciting, quest of all.”

It’s likely the oldest of the “7 Great Quests of Man,” as well. For as long as mankind has been aware that there was more beyond our world, we’ve wondered if there’s anybody out there. Unlike the other quests, your Bigfoots and Noah’s Arks—which call for some credulity, some willingness to believe the thing is possible—to many people, the idea that there must be some other intelligent life out in our vast universe feels so plausible that it’s hard not to resist. Yet, despite how improbable it seems that mankind is really alone in the universe, no credible evidence has ever materialized that there’s intelligent life out there.

A few years before our article was published, in 1972, Pioneer 10 took off from Cape Kennedy carrying a gold-covered plate with images of a man and a woman accompanied by diagrams that scientists hoped could be understood by any intelligent life it reached. It wasn’t the first attempt to contact alien life (Dr. Frank Drake launched Project Ozma back in 1960), but the legendary Carl Sagan thought this “message in a bottle” approach might be the key to communicating with intelligent life among the stars.

In the 21st century, the search for intelligent life continues unabated, be it attempts to identify aliens moving about in our universe today, or searching for remnants of those who may have died off far in the distant past. At Pop Mech, we’ve continued to keep our eyes to the skies, while trying to contend with the perplexing Fermi Paradox—the question of why, in a universe billions of years old, we appear to be the only intelligent life to ever exist in it.

Yet, with all our new technology developed in the last 50 years, we still find ourselves gazing up at the stars and wondering who might be out there, just as we did when “7 Great Quests of Man” was written.

Back then, we posited that our message would be heard by whatever life is out there. “It may happen a thousand years from now, or tomorrow.” We’ll check back in on that in another 50 years.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

#6384. Locusts may help scientists detect hard-to-treat lung infections

In lab tests, locusts could smell the difference between bacterial biofilms and free-floating bacteria, a finding that could inform future breath tests.

Bacteria become much harder to kill once they attach to a surface and build a slimy protective layer.

These colonies are called biofilms. No test can currently detect them in a patient’s lungs without an invasive procedure.

A locust’s sense of smell might help one day.

In lab tests, researchers used signals from locust brains to tell biofilms apart from free-floating bacteria of the same species by smell.

The clearest signal appeared about a second after the odor reached the locusts’ antennae.

Debajit Saha and Jonathan Hardy were the senior authors of the study. Both are associate professors at Michigan State University (MSU). Michael Parnas was the first author.

Saha works in the College of Engineering. Hardy is based in the Department of Microbiology, Genetics and Immunology. Both researchers also belong to MSU’s Institute for Quantitative Health Science and Engineering.

Only bacterial cultures grown in flasks were used. Breath samples and patients were not tested.

Saha noted that before the experiments, it was not clear that an odor alone could show how bacteria were growing.

“Seeing such a high level of discrimination was therefore quite surprising,” Saha said.

A biofilm forms when bacteria settle on a solid surface. A sticky coating is then built around the whole colony.

Inside that coating, bacteria can be up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics than free-floating bacteria. The authors gave that figure in the paper.

Some bacteria deep in the colony have a slower metabolism. Those cells can survive treatment, and the biofilm is rebuilt afterward.

Biofilms account for about 80% of bacterial infections in people, according to earlier research cited in the paper. Wounds, implants and the lungs can all be affected.

An infection is usually identified by growing a sample in a laboratory. That process takes a few days. Faster tests exist, but they cannot separate a biofilm from free-floating bacteria.

Bacteria also release chemicals into the air as they grow. Together, those airborne chemicals form an odor. An odor can be sampled from outside the body.

Locusts smell with their antennae. More than 100,000 odor-sensing nerve cells are found on each antenna.

The signals from those cells all pass through about 800 output neurons. These neurons are located in one small smell-processing region of the brain.

For the experiment, the brain was surgically exposed in six living locusts. Each insect was held still, and an electrode was placed in that region.

The team then blew air from five flasks across the antennae. Four flasks contained bacteria. The fifth contained only the broth in which the bacteria had been grown.

Two species were used, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Each species was grown in two ways, as a biofilm and as a free-floating culture.

Each odor was delivered for four seconds and repeated five times, with one minute between deliveries. The activity of 32 neurons was isolated from the recordings.

The locusts had not been trained on these odors. Insect brains have been used this way by Saha’s lab before. In earlier work, recordings were taken from locusts and honeybees exposed to the odors of human cancer cells.

Trained dogs can also detect some diseases by smell. However, a test based on an animal’s behavior gives only a yes or a no, the authors wrote.

A computer program compared the firing pattern from each trial with the patterns from the other trials. The closest match was then selected.

When all five odors were included, 22 of 25 trials were matched to the correct flask. That is an accuracy of 88%. Guessing would be right only 20% of the time.

Both biofilms were identified in every trial.

One of the five free-floating Staphylococcus trials was mistaken for the Staphylococcus biofilm. The plain broth was also mistaken for a Staphylococcus odor twice.

In this analysis, every biofilm was caught by the program. One free-floating sample was wrongly flagged as a biofilm, however.

The researchers reported accuracy of up to 96% when individual biofilm and free-floating odors were classified.

The largest differences in firing patterns were seen between the two species. Biofilm and free-floating cultures of the same species produced more similar patterns. Even so, they were still separated by the recordings.

Saha said bacteria release a different mix of airborne chemicals when their growth state changes. These subtle changes can be picked up by the insects.

Before the odor arrived, the program performed no better than guessing. Accuracy rose quickly once the odor was delivered.

The team then tested how little brain activity was needed. A half-second slice of the recording was enough for 91% accuracy. That slice was centered about one second after the odor arrived.

A quarter-second slice from the same moment gave 82% accuracy. A laboratory culture, by comparison, takes days.

The 32 neurons represent about 4% of the roughly 800 output neurons in the smell-processing region. The biofilm analysis was also repeated on random subsets of the 32.

Performance improved as more neurons were included.

Only one laboratory strain of each species was used. Human breath is more complicated. It also carries chemicals from food, medications and the surrounding air.

Several other limits were listed by the authors. The number of bacteria could not be kept exactly equal in the biofilm and free-floating flasks. That difference alone could change an odor.

All 32 neurons were pooled from six insects. The study therefore does not show a single locust doing the job.

The recordings stayed strong for about four hours after surgery. How long a locust lasts as a sensor depends on its health and the surgeon’s skill, the authors wrote.

Drug-resistant strains such as MRSA were not tested either. The team expects those strains to be harder to distinguish from ordinary Staphylococcus.

No one has yet tested whether a locust brain can pick a biofilm’s odor out of human breath.

Breath studies are the next step, the authors wrote. Hardy said the team is interested in testing breath samples from children with cystic fibrosis. Persistent lung infections that involve biofilms can develop in these children.

Pseudomonas is a major cause of lung infections in people with the disease, according to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.

Custom electrodes are also being developed so that enough data can be collected from a single locust.

In the long term, the researchers want to build a portable sensor. It would connect a living locust’s smell system to small electronics and artificial intelligence.

More bacterial species and samples from patients will be needed in future work. The results will also have to be compared with the laboratory methods already used in hospitals.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."
